examples: Since they're only children, please be lenient with them.
As it was my first time, I handled things clumsily. Please forgive me.
Not knowing the circumstances, I said something I should not have.
Because of a sudden business trip, I was unable even to say goodbye. My apologies.
As I am not used to this yet, I will need a little time.
fields.explain:
Nuance: humble, asking for forgiveness, explaining an unavoidable cause.
Position: usually at the beginning of a sentence to state the reason, followed by an apology/request.
Suitable for business emails, official notices, and speeches.
Combinations: often used with apologetic keigo phrases such as 失礼いたしました,申し訳ございません.

～こととて means “because/since it is … ”, used to state a circumstantial reason and ask for understanding/forgiveness. It is a classical, formal expression, often seen in written language, apologies, and notices.
• Usually follows N denoting a situation: 子ども, 初めて, 不慣れ, 急用, 留守, 多忙.
• What follows ～こととて is usually a clause asking for understanding, expressing an unavoidable result.
• Rarely used in everyday conversation; replaced by ～ものですから, ～もので, ～ため.
• Not used directly with commands/strong resolutions; suitable for asking permission, apologizing, and explaining.
fields.notes:
• “こととて” comes from “こと（事）+とて（と言って）”, with a nuance like “saying that it is …, so”.
• Formulaic: 子どものこととて, 初めてのこととて are almost fixed phrases.
• Often accompanied by keigo/humble language to keep the style consistent.
• In literature/parallel prose, used to create an old-fashioned, polite tone.
mistakes: Using it in casual conversation sounds stiff and affected; use ～もので instead.
Attaching it directly to the dictionary form of a verb is sometimes awkward; prefer Nのこととて or a shortened clause.
JLPT: a trap distinguishing the nuance of asking forgiveness (～こととて) from the neutral one (～ため). If the sentence has 失礼/ご容赦ください → choose ～こととて.
Not used for commands/strong volition: ～こととて, 行け is unnatural.

examples: Ever since my child was born, I've hardly gone out drinking.
Ever since I moved to this town, I've been using the car much more often.
Ever since I witnessed that accident, I haven't been able to walk alone at night.
Ever since we got a new boss, overtime has become the norm.
Ever since I changed my smartphone, I can't get enough of taking photos.
fields.explain:
Used when you want to emphasize a change that has lasted since a certain point.
The subject is usually the speaker or a close group, since it involves subjective perception.
Rarely used with a direct command/intention in the second clause.
Often used with the negative to emphasize “no longer doing X”: ～なくなった／とんと～ない.

～てからというもの emphasizes that, from a certain point in time/action that serves as a marker, the situation in the following clause changed markedly and continues to the present.
• Often accompanied by words of duration: ずっと／めっきり／とんと～ない／まったく～ない.
• The second clause is usually a habit/state, rarely a single action that ends immediately.
• Has a stronger emotional/subjective nuance than ～て以来, suggesting “from then on, everything was different”.
• Not used for very short time spans or trivial everyday events.
fields.notes:
• The second clause is often in the present/present perfect in the Japanese sense (～ている／～なくなる).
• Works well in written language, narratives about life, and essays about turning points.
• Can follow social events: 震災／コロナ禍／不況 からというもの、～
mistakes: Using it for a brief, one-time event in the second clause → wrong nuance (it must be a lasting state).
Confusing it with ～てから: that lacks the sense of “completely changed and lasting”.
Using it with a trivial reference point (e.g., 昨日～) → unnatural.
Attaching a direct command/volition in the second clause → inappropriate.

Since X, the situation has changed markedly and lasted
Emphasizes a change to “something completely different”

examples: I sincerely wish you all good health and happiness.
I pray with all my heart for the swift recovery of the disaster-stricken areas.
I love my hometown dearly.
I have the highest hopes for the arrival of a new era.
I pray earnestly that my late friend may rest in peace.
fields.explain:
Suitable for well-wishes, formal speeches, and reflective writing.
Rarely used with concrete action verbs; mainly with verbs of mental state.
Can be used as a modifier:私の 愛してやまない 家族.
Not used for momentary emotions like驚く,怒る in an outburst sense.

• Expresses feelings, wishes, or inner attitudes that are “unceasing, never fading” and enduring.
• Usually used with psychological/emotional verbs: 願う, 期待する, 愛する, 慕う, 祈る, 尊敬する.
• Formal nuance, often used in written language, speeches, eulogies, and well-wishes.
• The subject is usually the speaker or a representative speaker; rarely used for strong, sudden negative emotions.
fields.notes:
• The pattern often appears with formal nouns: ご健康, ご多幸, 平和, 復興.
• 愛してやまない can be used as a modifier to emphasize a special degree of affection.
• The polite form ～てやみません suits business correspondence and eulogies.
mistakes: Using it with concrete action verbs (行く, 食べる): unnatural.
Using it for sudden emotions: wrong nuance; use ～てたまらない/～てならない instead.
Dropping を before a psychological verb: you need Nを願ってやまない/期待してやまない.
Wrong tense: ～てやまない is usually in the present to express lasting feelings; the past is rare.

Different, spontaneous nuance; often with <ruby>感<rt>かん</rt></ruby>じる/<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>える/<ruby>心配<rt>しんぱい</rt></ruby>だ.
Strong, leaning toward physical sensations/sudden emotions.
Neutral in nuance; describes duration, not formal.

fields.meaning: If not…, then what is it?
examples: The whole family came home safely. If this isn't happiness, what is?
Thirty years of research have borne fruit. If this isn't truly the fruit of hard work, what is?
A single spring welling up in the wilderness: if that isn't a miracle, what is?
If this tranquility and harmony isn't art, what is?
What he did, protecting it at the risk of his life: if that isn't courage, what is?
The bond with friends who overcame hard times together: if this isn't love, what is?
fields.explain:
Used in emotional writing, speeches, and editorials; rarely used in ordinary conversation.
Usually placed after “これが／それは／まさに／こそ”.
Not used to ask for real information; it is a rhetorical question meant to affirm.

• A rhetorical question for strong affirmation: “if it is not …, then what else is it?”.
• Expresses deep emotion toward something rare/precious/moving.
• Usually used with abstract nouns: 幸せ・愛・奇跡・努力の結晶・芸術・誇り…
fields.notes:
• With i-adjectives, nominalize them: 美しい → 美しさ／美 → 美でなくてなんだろう.
• Often combined with まさに／こそ to increase expressive force.
• Sometimes “か” is added at the end of the sentence: ～でなくてなんだろうか (softer).
mistakes: Using it with an i-adjective in the dictionary form: × 嬉しくなくてなんだろう → use 名詞化 instead: 喜びでなくてなんだろう.
Understanding it as a real question awaiting an answer; it is actually a rhetorical affirmation.
Using it in everyday situations makes the sentence overly dramatic and unnatural.

examples: You're not a child, so don't cry over something like that.
It's not as if this is a joke. I can't pay that kind of money!
You're not an amateur, so I'd like you to avoid basic mistakes.
You're not a student anymore, so stop staying up all night playing games.
It's not a day off, so don't come to the office dressed so casually.
fields.explain:
Used when the speaker thinks that, “since it is not N”, the behavior/demand in the second clause is inappropriate.
The second clause is usually: a command (～しろ/するな), a request (～してくれ), a critical evaluation (～のはおかしい/だめだ), or advice (～ほうがいい).
The style is somewhat stiff and can sound reproachful; avoid using it with superiors or in very polite contexts.
The variant じゃあるまいし is colloquial and natural in conversation.

- Meaning: “It's not as if it's N, so…”, “It's not N, so (don't/no need to) …”. Used to gently reproach, admonish, or reject excessive behavior/standards by giving the reason “it is not N”.
- Nuance: Fairly strong, critical/admonishing. Usually followed by a command, prohibition, or advice in the second clause. Sounds somewhat old-fashioned, with a masculine/mature tone.
- Range of combination: Mainly attaches to nouns denoting a status/state used for contrast (子供、素人、学生、冗談…). Use with a clause is an extended variant, so use it with care.
fields.notes:
• Often appears in written language, speeches, or “mature” criticism. In casual conversation, consider the softer version: ～ではないんだから.
• The preceding noun should be a category whose opposite everyone understands (子供/大人, 冗談/本気, 素人/プロ…).
• Not used to describe a purely objective fact; it must carry an evaluation/implication of correcting behavior.
mistakes: Using it directly with verbs/adjectives: Incorrect; this pattern attaches to nouns. With a clause, switch to ～というわけではあるまいし.
Confusing it with ～ではあるまいか (conjecture). The two patterns have different meanings.
Using it in polite contexts with superiors can be rude because of its reproachful nuance.
JLPT: a trap of choosing between “～ではないんだから” and “～ではあるまいし” based on formality/nuance.

fields.meaning: Cannot be let go with just…
fields.connection: V (plain form) + (の) + ではすまない ではすまされない / N
examples: If it turns out you leaked confidential information, an apology won't be enough.
This accident is a serious problem that can't be settled with just a warning.
The repairs will probably cost more than a few tens of thousands of yen.
If you damage public property, compensation alone may not be enough to settle it.
If you are this late, you may get more than just a verbal warning.
fields.explain:
Follows N denoting a mild measure/form of handling, to say it is “not enough”.
A critical, stern tone; suits written language or firm statements.
The passive variant ～では済まされない emphasizes that it cannot be overlooked.

• Expresses seriousness: something cannot be resolved/ended with just measure N (an apology, a warning, a small fine…).
• An objective/somewhat formal evaluation; often used in the news, written language, and serious criticism.
• Often used with nouns such as: 謝罪, 弁償, 注意, 罰金, 処分, 数量表現, この程度.
fields.notes:
• N1–N2. The JLPT often sets traps with “Vないではすまない/ずにはすまない”.
• Kanji variant: 済む/済まない is common in written language.
• Used with counters to exaggerate the extent of damage/cost.
mistakes: Using it directly with a verb: “謝ってではすまない” × → “謝罪ではすまない” ○ (nominalization).
Confusing it with “Vないではすまない” (meaning you must do it), which is completely different in structure and meaning.
Without context showing the seriousness, the sentence sounds exaggerated; state the consequence/measure.
Mixing up 済む/住む (different kanji with different meanings).

rows: N is a mild measure, which is negated
<ruby>謝罪<rt>しゃざい</rt></ruby>ではすまない
Different grammar; says “it won't do unless you do it”
<ruby>謝<rt>あやま</rt></ruby>らないではすまない
Not about handling something, but about circumstances not allowing it
<ruby>注意<rt>ちゅうい</rt></ruby>だけで<ruby>済<rt>す</rt></ruby>む

fields.connection: V (plain form) + とあれば / N / Na / Aい
examples: If it's for my children, I'm willing to endure any hardship.
If it's a request from you, I'll gladly accept.
If necessary, I'll rush over even in the middle of the night.
If it's for the future of the company, reform is unavoidable.
If it's about him, everyone will probably cooperate.
fields.explain:
The second clause usually expresses volition/determination/an evaluation of high likelihood.
Used when the condition has special value:子ども、恩人、緊急、必要、国益…
More formal than ～なら; a rhetorical/resolute nuance.

• If (it really is) …, then (I/we) will …; the condition is special or worth making sacrifices for.
• Emphasizes determination/readiness to do something difficult/unusual for a great purpose.
• Often used in formal spoken language/advertising/declarations.
fields.notes:
• N2–N1. Often seen in slogans/internal rules of a declarative nature.
• Readily used in fixed phrases: 必要とあれば／あなたの頼みとあれば／子どものためとあれば.
• The second clause sometimes uses the passive/natural form: ～だろう for strong conjecture.
mistakes: In natural writing, the second clause cannot be a direct command to the listener; use the speaker's volitional/declarative form instead.
Confusing it with ～とあって: one is a condition (volition), the other a cause (narration).
Applying it to an ordinary condition makes the sentence sound exaggerated; choose a “special” condition.

fields.connection: N (unit of time) + というもの
examples: For this past month, I haven't been able to get any proper rest.
For the three days before the exam, I shut myself up in the library every day.
Learn some manners.
I don't have any special talent to speak of, but I'm confident in my perseverance.
As a working adult, it goes without saying that you should be punctual.
For these two years, I haven't heard a word from him.
fields.explain:
Duration meaning: Usually used with negative/difficult expressions (～ない、～できない、～ばかりだ…). Used for a period of time that has lasted up to the present.
Defining meaning: Emphasizes a standard, with a generalizing nuance, sometimes critical.
Formality: Fairly formal; often found in written language/essays.

• Meaning 1 (duration): “For the whole … (just past)”, emphasizing continuity up to the present, often with a nuance of complaint/difficulty/absence.
• Meaning 2 (definition/emphasis): “What is called …/the thing known as …”, used to state the essence, a standard, or something worthy of being called X.
• Pragmatics: Meaning 1 leans toward written language/description; meaning 2 is used in explanations, criticism, or stating general standards.
fields.notes:
• “Time span + というもの” is often linked with negative emotions or an unusual state that has continued.
• With “これというもの”: usually used with the negative to say “there is nothing decent/worth mentioning”.
• Put “というもの” after an abstract noun (礼儀、常識、誠意…) to emphasize a social standard.
mistakes: Confusing it with ～というものだ: one is “definition/judgment”, the other is “duration”. Look at the following verb to tell them apart.
Using it with a future time span is incorrect: you cannot say ×来月というもの. It is used only for a period that “has passed” up to the present.
Dropping the negative nuance in the duration meaning: a neutral sentence tends to sound awkward. Use it with a negative/difficulty.

rows: Neutral; does not necessarily last up to the “present moment of speaking”.
<ruby>休暇<rt>きゅうか</rt></ruby>の<ruby>間<rt>ま</rt></ruby>よく<ruby>眠<rt>ねむ</rt></ruby>った。

A different pattern: judgment/moral principle, not “duration”.
<ruby>遅刻<rt>ちこく</rt></ruby>は<ruby>失礼<rt>しつれい</rt></ruby>というものだ。
Negative form of judgment; easily confused with “というもの”.

fields.connection: V (plain form) + といえ(ども) / N + (だ) / Na + (だ) / Aい + い
examples: Even a child must not harm others.
No matter how busy you are, you must not neglect your health.
Even professionals make mistakes.
Even though you are a student, you need to be aware that you are a member of society.
No matter how old you are, you can grow as long as you are willing to learn.
Even in wartime, human rights should be protected.
fields.explain:
A stiff, rational nuance; avoid it in everyday casual conversation (use とはいえ/といっても instead).
Suitable for stating principles/standards, legal rules, morals, and public statements.
The following clause usually means “no exceptions/must not/cannot/naturally…”.
Emphasis with いかに/たとえ ⇒ strong concession.

- A formal concession pattern: “Even if/even though … (still) …”. It presents a strong fact/condition, but the following clause negates the expectation or affirms an unchanging principle.
• Highly formal (written language, speeches, essays, news).
• Often used with N denoting a status or general attribute: 天才・プロ・子ども・政府・法律… to say “even … is no exception”.
• Common accompanying adverbs: たとえ, いかに, どれほど, 誰・何・いつ + といえども (whoever/whatever/whenever…).
• The following clause usually contains a normative judgment, a firm command, or something that does not change.
fields.notes:
• Common emphatic phrases: 誰といえども (anyone at all), 何人といえども (whoever it may be), いかに/どれほど + Adj/Adv + といえども.
• Old-fashioned/legal/speech style: appears often in policy documents and speeches.
• Strongly negates expectations: often used to create a “no exceptions” stance, suitable for argumentation.
mistakes: Using it in casual conversation → sounds awkward: switch to とはいえ/といっても.
Wrongly attaching “だ”: with N/na, だ is usually dropped before といえども; use である for formality: 正) 学生であるといえども; 子どもといえども.
The following clause should not be an unrelated, incidental event: it needs to be a conclusion/standard that goes against expectations.
Confusing its meaning with とはいえ: exam questions often test the degree of formality and the range of combination.
